newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee plummets, corrects after 3-day run-up.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee plummets, corrects after 3-day run-up.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures' explosive three-day rally came to an abrupt halt on Friday, as frantic speculative selling sent the benchmark July contract plummeting 12 percent, traders said.
In what the exchange said was coffee's largest one-day decline on record, July arabicas tumbled 38.40 cents per lb, to 276.40 cents, after ranging between 311.00 and 273.00.
Second-month September plunged 35.50 cents, to 238.30 cents, while the back months dropped 23.15 to 28.40.
"It's foolish to think a market goes in only one direction," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "When it rises that much, the pull backs are going to be more severe.
"Moves like this take your breath away," she added.

The past three sessions have also been breathtaking, with July surging a whopping 57.95 cents -- or more than 22 percent -- to peak at a lifetime high of 318.00 cents a lb, a level not seen in 20 years.
"The specs got ahead of themselves and they lost control," said one trader. "It's the end of the month and it made the market ripe for a sell-off."
Coffee prices gapped lower from the outset on Friday, as speculators moved to take profits. Traders said a report from U.K. trade house ED&F Man may have set a bearish tone.
In its April/May coffee report, Man said world consumer coffee stocks stood at 10 million bags in April, up from 8.80 million in March and 1.1 million bags higher than in April 1996.
While growth has been concentrated in European ports, Man said U.S. stocks increased by 309,000 bags in the last two months to stand at 1.85 million bags.

"The ED&F Man report, which showed a stock increase of 1.1 million bags, may have weighed on the market," said Ganes. "But it should not have been a surprise because it reflected a period of high shipments."
Also dampening sentiment was news private exporters in Colombia were having a hard time finding buyers for about 300,000 60-kg bags of green coffee for shipment in June.

Exporters, who orininally offered the coffee to European and Japanese roasters, said there have been no takers for the coffee in North America because it is priced against the expensive July contract.

"The roasters are backing off on June purchases even though the Colombians increased supplies to the U.S. and Canada," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "Nobody wants to touch it at this price and they're saying,"I don't have to buy."
But despite today's massive sell-off may have taken shaken up some of the bulls, traders and analysts said the fundamental picture was likely to inspire another move to the upside.
"The problem isn't over," said Merill Lynch's Ganes. "It is still a very tight situation going into the frost season in Brazil."
